segments: Docker helped popularize container image distribution and development workflows, and helped establish the OCI standards. Understanding its client–server architecture is the starting point for understanding every Docker operation.
What is a container? A beginner's introduction

If you have already read the container introduction in the Podman series The basic concepts are explained in detail in Podman 01. Docker and Podman use the same container standards (OCI), so their fundamental concepts are shared, although the engines differ in specific features.
Images and containers
Image: a read-only template containing everything needed to run a program: code, libraries, and configuration files. Think of it as the "installation package".
Container: a running instance of an image. Think of it as the "running program".
Client–server architecture: Docker's core model
What happens at each step:
You enter docker run nginx:alpine
The docker CLI sends a request to /var/run/docker.sock
dockerd (the daemon) receives the request and checks whether the nginx:alpine image is available locally; if not, it pulls the image from Docker Hub
dockerd calls containerd to create the container
containerd calls runc to start the container process
Your nginx container starts running. The actual process-parent relationships involve the containerd shim and runtime; the container process cannot simply be described as a direct child of dockerd
Three key components
dockerd (the daemon)
Always running in the background: starts automatically at system boot and continues to occupy memory
rootful or rootless: the traditional system daemon runs as root, but rootless operation can also be configured. Permission to control a rootful socket should be treated as privileged access
Centralized control: this article describes the traditional daemon-managed path. Builds and different contexts may involve additional tools and services

Management becomes unavailable; existing container behavior depends on settings such as live-restore: an unavailable daemon affects management operations. live-restore can keep standalone containers running during some daemon shutdowns/upgrades, subject to version and log-buffer limits
docker.sock (the communication bridge)
/var/run/docker.sock is dockerd's Unix socket file:
Docker Hub (the image registry)
Docker Hub (docker.io) is Docker's public image registry, similar to GitHub but for images:
docker pull nginx:alpine pulls from Docker Hub by default
You can also push your own images: docker push exampleuser/myimage:latest
In mainland China, you may need a registry mirror for faster access (configure registry-mirrors)

Docker and the OCI standards
In 2015, Docker donated the runc container runtime to the OCI (Open Container Initiative). OCI defines specifications for images, runtimes, distribution, and more. Two are relevant here:
OCI Image Spec — the image format standard (Docker supports OCI and related image formats; check the specific manifest/media type)
OCI Runtime Spec — the container runtime standard (runc is the reference implementation)

What this means: common compatible images can be used by Podman or the container engines used by Kubernetes, but they must still match the platform architecture, runtime requirements, and configuration. containerd itself also needs the appropriate tools and configuration. The image format is not proprietary to Docker.
